text: This button can have six different states. This is part 17 of my Build For Good UX series. You use buttons every single day across all kinds of apps on your phone, on your computer. And you probably don't notice the subtle button states that can change how this experience feels for you. So let's go through them. First, this is the default state. The button looks like it can be pressed. There are different ways to design to look this way, but usually it's a solid fill, a clear outline, and maybe a soft shadow that makes it looks slightly raised. Now this is a bad example. Next, we have the hover state. This is when your cursor hovers over a button and there's a slight visual change. Usually with the color or the outline, it sends a signal to your brain saying, "I'm interactive, I will respond if you click." But this only works on your computer because on your phone, you don't have a cursor to hover. And if you try to implement a hover on mobile, it turns out looking like this, which is confusing and buggy. Next, the focus state. This one is super important for accessibility for anyone navigating with a screen reader or a keyboard. You hit tap to jump between elements and you should see this outline to know exactly what button you're on. Okay, now you press the button. This is the pressed state. Here you should see your feel some kind of feedback that your tap did something. On a computer, the button might darken or might have some kind of animation to make it look like the button got pushed in. On your phone, there's sometimes a tiny little half tick buzz or a ripple. We take this state completely for granted because if there was zero feedback at this point, this is where people start pressing the button again and again because they assume the site is frozen or not responding. Next, we have the loading state, which gets kicked off right after the press state. And it's the button telling you, "Hey, you click something "and now I'm working in the background to actually make it happen." And putting the loader right inside the button is convenient because it's already where you're looking and it doesn't disrupt the whole page with a full screen loader. And last, we have the disabled state where the button is not available. Usually it's just gray color and it looks like something you can't press. There's actually debate on whether disabled buttons are considered a bad practice these days so I will be getting into that in the next part. So follow for more.
